speaker: williamponall
text: I think there's significant evidence or there would be legally sufficient evidence to support a conviction of burglary based on the facts in this case. There was no evidence that both these individuals and like in Midget, the defense was misidentification that he was not the individual that robbed, burglarized his house. So I think there's a difference between legally sufficient evidence for conviction and whether they should have got the inference instruction. speaker: edwards

speaker: edwards

If it's not fundamental error, we believe it's ineffective on its face because there's no legitimate reason for trial counsel not to object to this instruction based on the evidence in this case. There will be, I can't conceive of, and I don't think anyone can conceive of a situation where you want the jury to hear even a permissive inference that your defendant is guilty if you could prevent it. So.

speaker: edwards
text: But to follow through on that, wouldn't we have to find that the court would have granted the objection to that jury instruction?

text: Of course, of course. You have to agree with my argument that under the case law, the instruction was inappropriate. So I certainly agree with that. I mean, I think on a deficiency prong, I think certainly it'd be hard to argue there was not a viable argument against the instruction, but as far as prejudice, I think you would have to find that the instruction was improperly given. So, and we don't have any testimony or evidence about the identity of the other individual. And again, we have a misidentification defense like we did in Midget. So it's our position that the evidence is not sufficient to show that they're acting in concert to commit this alleged burglary. So for those reasons, we'd ask that the court reverse his conviction and remand for a new trial without the inference instruction.

text: May it please the court. My name is Richard Powis. I represent the state of Florida. It's our position simply that this was a valid instruction. It was proper for the trial court to give it. And of course, this container was found with change spilled out on the floor. Real quick to touch upon Midget. That case was a 3850 case regarding ineffective assistance of counsel. And this court was only ruling that it was a facially sufficient claim by stating that the defendant in Midget was only in the vicinity of where the burgled area was or where the property was found. Here, we have much more than that. We're not just in the vicinity of a building. We're shown actually entering property through the backyard. Of course, law enforcement confirmed soon after the defendant left that the window was broken. A rock was later found on the bed at a later time, likely used to break this. And the victim identified this particular container. I think that's a perfect inference that this container was taken from there. And to touch upon acting in concert, it was observed by, I believe it was not Deputy Fisher. It would have been a Deputy Bennett. He saw the defendant exit the vehicle and approach the victim's home, enter the victim's home. When he saw him leave 30 minutes later, he testified that the vehicle actually pulled up to him, showing that I don't believe this white SUV was a self-driving car. Likely the passenger was obviously the person who brought this vehicle forward. And then he must've moved over back in the passenger seat because everyone observed the defendant driving the vehicle later on, especially at that time when he left. I think that as the case law has said, and I believe it's A-L, just because there's two people in the car doesn't mean the defendant is, this instruction's improper. In most of those cases, we don't have this evidence here. There's no evidence usually leaking or linking the actual defendants on the property. In the Dobbins case, cited an appellant's reply brief, this defendant did not actually, I'm sorry, no one actually testified that they saw him at the property when any of these burglaries were committed. They only found the other passenger who was arrested at a later time. And it's important that that all happened in the span, he was pulled over about a week or a few weeks after the burglary was reported. And then people were found there again months later. He wasn't arrested until the DNA testing was done. And it was on one cigarette, and it's possible he could have just trespassed and left the cigarette with his DNA there. I don't think that that case is at all analogous to this because he was apprehended in less than an hour. They saw him go in at 12, he left at 12.30. Deputy, forgive me for pronouncing this wrong, but Cesney sees him driving the vehicle during law enforcement's pursuit of him around 12.30. And of course, Mr. Fisher, Deputy Fisher, identifies him as the same person he saw at 4.30 and 12 o'clock being apprehended around 1 p.m. And just to touch real quick on prejudice and the effectiveness on the face of the record, I mean, this is an abuse of discretion standard. I mean, the trial court ruling on that is presumed correct. So had this objection been logged, he's going to look whether the facts support the instruction, whether it's a proper instruction, and then whether it's necessary for the jury. I believe there's no reasonable probability the court would rule any differently, and certainly no reasonable probability an appellate court would rule any differently based on the facts that were derived in this case. And further, just to touch upon fundamental error, a majority instruction was rise to this. The Heathcote case is using a completely incorrect instruction. In that one, it was an attempt to commit an attempted sexual battery. And in the Yee case, it left out that a touching was done in a lewd and lascivious manner. Those are incorrect instructions, whereas this is an instruction that's been given since 1885. If there are no other questions, I will rely on my brief, and I ask that you affirm.

To the extent that the state is arguing that the two individuals in the car were acting in concert, it's well-established that mere presence at the scene of a crime without more is not evidence of principal liability or accomplice liability. So without more evidence that this other person helped in the planning or execution of this burglary, I don't think you could conclude that that person was acting in concert to justify this instruction.
